channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Over 40 items and £60,000: the Friends of the Falklands Museum launch their website
item.description: MercoPress: “The UK charity that acquires and sends Falklands heritage items to the archipelago has launched a new website after securing more than 40 objects, documents and books for Stanley’s historical institutions over the past decade.”

item.title: Maproom Blog
item.description: Found via Mapping Tariffs. “Since May 2025, Tara Vinodrai and Karen Chapple have led a team of researchers at the School of Cities to develop interactive mapping and visualization tools that measure and explore the potential impacts of tariffs on jobs and businesses across Canadian cities and communities at the neighbourhood and city level.”

item.title: Innovations in Mali Cataloging Work
item.description: Hill Museum & Manuscript Library: “HMML’s decade-long project in Mali digitized more than 300,000 manuscripts, amounting to an estimated 4.35 million unique image files (such as page 1 of SAV BAB 01076, pictured above). An incredible testament to the region’s ancient and ongoing manuscript culture, it was also a seemingly insurmountable task for the two catalogers of West African manuscripts at HMML, Dr. Ali Diakite and Dr. Paul Naylor.”

item.title: Here’s Everything You Need to Know About Mighty Mike Plays and the $118,000 He Allegedly Cost His Dad
item.description: IGN: “For every viewer who feels for Dave and the rest of the Mighty Mike family, there’s someone who’s concerned that the mass amount of attention is part of a grand scheme to garner attention…. Now, scam allegations have cropped up online as some look to the channel to come up with a better explanation. Dave’s willingness to use a company card on Robux was enough to raise a few eyebrows, while others questioned how his unnamed employer could allow Mighty Mike to rack up a $118,000 bill without anyone catching on sooner.”

item.title: 7 ways to get free movies and TV channels on your smart TV
item.description: Engadget: “With how many paid streaming services there are, you’d be forgiven for thinking you have to pay to watch high-quality movies and TV. But thankfully, this isn’t the case at all. If you look around a bit, you’ll find tons of free streaming options with more than you could ever hope to watch. Most provide two formats: a standard on-demand library to choose from, alongside a channel-surfing experience that mimics the old days of cable.”

item.title: WCM Ukraine Expands Documentation Partnerships
item.description: War Childhood Museum: “The War Childhood Museum Ukraine is expanding its work to document and preserve childhood experiences of the Russian-Ukrainian War through two new collaborations: a partnership with the Ukraine War Archive and a new documentation initiative within the ‘People of the Future’ project.”

item.title: Reanimating a Corpus. Or Two. Or More.
item.description: Doc Searls: “For many years, I have despaired of ever saving the contents of my old blog (1999-2007), my writing for Linux Journal (1996-2019), and countless other articles, essays, and posts, published mostly on the Web—which looks and sounds like a permanent place (‘sites,’ ‘locations,’ ‘domains’), but in fact is a whiteboard. Then, last week, I asked Claude for help. I pay Anthropic $20/month* for Claude’s services (Sonnet 5 at the moment), and it successfully rescued both my old blog and every item I ever submitted to Linux Journal. They are now at searls.com.”

item.title: At 10 Years, DolphinWatch Faces Its Big Question: How Many?
item.description: Southern Maryland Chronicle: “Chesapeake DolphinWatch, the citizen-science app that lets Bay boaters and shoreline watchers report bottlenose dolphin sightings, is marking its tenth year with more than 20,000 users and over 12,000 logged sightings — and with researchers turning to new tools to answer the one question the app can’t: how many dolphins actually live in the Chesapeake Bay.”

item.title: Why I Stay Off Twitter
item.description: Jeff Kaufman: “After staying off Twitter reasonably successfully for years, I cross-posted my AI Tweets there a few weeks ago. I had something very Twitter-shaped to say, and I thought it was important to get out, so I do think this was worth it. And it all went well: none of this is complaining about the comments I got there. Coming back a few times to check notifications, however, it’s been very good at baiting me: Tweets that are confidently wrong in cases where I have relevant and uncommon knowledge.”

item.title: Indigenous screen organisations from Canada, Aotearoa New Zealand and Australia launch new international co-production initiative
item.description: Screen Australia: “Shared Ground will connect Indigenous filmmakers across three countries through a series of international labs designed to build relationships and create new opportunities for Indigenous-led collaboration.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: New Database Highlights City Climate Policies in Over 150 of the Largest U.S. Cities
item.description: University of Maryland: “Detailing more than 1,400 climate and energy policies and programs enacted by 157 major U.S. cities across 48 states, the actions taken by cities improve health, reduce emissions, and increase energy efficiency and affordability across the buildings, transportation, and electricity sectors, among others.”

item.title: Harvard launches tool tracking corporate climate targets in U.S. public markets
item.description: Harvard University: “Do voluntary corporate climate targets reduce greenhouse gas emissions? How have these targets evolved over the last few decades? When a firm announces a target, does its behavior change? The Salata Institute today launches the Corporate Climate Targets Database, a free interactive tool designed to help answer those questions and fill critical gaps in the available data. It tracks voluntary climate targets, corporate emissions, and how they have changed over more than 20 years.”

item.title: How Amateur Naturalists Are Helping Scientists Track What Everything Eats
item.description: North Carolina State University: “An interdisciplinary team of researchers has created an open-source website to learn what different organisms eat, and what eats them. The site – called Who Eats Whom – draws on data from a worldwide citizen science platform and serves as both a valuable resource for ecological research and an educational tool to advance public understanding of the global food web.”

item.title: Ubuntu wiki gets its first overhaul in 16 years
item.description: OMG Ubuntu: “An all-new Ubuntu Wiki has gone live, giving the information hub its first substantive overhaul since 2010. The updated wiki now runs on MediaWiki, which adds a slate of modern backend and frontend features readers and editors alike will appreciate, e.g., search auto-suggest, mobile-friendly adaptations, light/dark mode, a WYSIWYG editor and more.” The old content has been archived.

item.title: Google Appeals $425M Privacy Verdict
item.description: MediaPost: “Google has taken the first step toward appealing a ruling requiring the company to pay $425 million for allegedly violating mobile users’ privacy. The company — which filed a ‘notice of appeal’ Monday — has not yet madesubstantive arguments to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which will hear the case.”

item.title: UNT removes webpage about LGBTQ library archives after North Texas lawmaker’s posts
item.description: Dallas Morning News: “The University of North Texas has erased a webpage about its LGBTQ archival collection after a state lawmaker called for its removal, according to online records. UNT’s library stores and archives one of the largest collections of LGBTQ history in North Texas.”

item.title: Google fully details Googlebooks: $899+, October launch, & more
item.description: 9to5 Google: “Following the May preview, Google today fully announced Googlebooks ahead of the consumer launch in October.”

item.title: How long can you expect your old cassette tapes to last?
item.description: Engadget: “If you grew up in the 1980s, chances are you had a collection of cassette tapes. Remember those? The media format, about the size of a large stack of credit cards, was the primary way we listened to music in the ’80s before being overtaken by CDs in the ’90s and eventually streaming services like Spotify. If you’re like me, you may still have many of them stored in a shoebox. But how long are these tiny tapes expected to last?”

item.title: California tightens disclosure rules for influencers who post political ads
item.description: NBC News: “California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill imposing criminal and civil penalties on content creators who fail to disclose paid political advertisements, a measure aimed at bringing greater transparency to the growing use of influencer marketing in politics.”

item.title: Foreign Journalists Seeking U.S. Visas Must Make Social Media Public Starting Oct. 1
item.description: NepYork: “Foreign journalists applying for U.S. media visas will be required to make their social media accounts publicly viewable beginning Oct. 1 under an expanded visa-screening policy announced by the U.S. State Department.”

item.title: How AP obtained and analyzed data on 4.5 million migrants released in the US at the border
item.description: Associated Press: “Newly obtained data on the unprecedented surge of border crossings over the past decade is shedding light on who entered the U.S. and where they went. Here is some information on the crossings, the data on 4.5 million migrants, and how The Associated Press obtained and analyzed it.”

item.title: Building an Urban Heat Island Detector with Python, Satellite Data, and Machine Learning
item.description: HackerNoon: “Every summer, cities get hotter than the countryside around them. This isn’t just a feeling; it’s a measurable phenomenon called the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, where concrete, asphalt, and dense buildings trap heat that green spaces and water bodies would otherwise dissipate… As a data analyst, and I also lecture on machine learning at university level, so this is the kind of question I like poking at outside of work: can we use free satellite data and a fairly ordinary machine learning pipeline to map heat islands in any city, without expensive proprietary tools?” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New website gives Earth its own video game-style patch notes
item.description: Dexerto: “It showcases unlocked features, added discoveries, updates like new satellites or restocked inventories, and even nerfs, highlighting high energy costs and health disasters like pandemics or positive things for humans like the recent elimination of Trachoma in Southeast Asia. The site itself is fairly new, with the developer detailing that they wanted to focus on the positive changes the world is making, while also tackling any doomscrolling, allowing users to see any large developments in the world, and when they happen, alongside sources and more details on the ‘patch’.”

item.title: Belarus Creates Large Digital Library on Tree Beekeeping
item.description: Nasa Niva: “Public access has opened in Belarus to ‘The Great Tree Beekeeping Library’ — a digital research corpus dedicated to the history and culture of tree beekeeping…. The project’s analytical card index contains about 1200 pages and more than 334 thousand words. More than a thousand other found sources are awaiting processing. The materials are presented in Belarusian, Russian, Polish, Ukrainian, and English.”

item.title: OCLC’s new CONTENTdm helps libraries and other institutions expand the reach of unique collections
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “OCLC has introduced a new version of the CONTENTdm digital collection management platform that empowers libraries, archives, and museums to make their unique digital collections more visible, accessible, and connected.”

item.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
item.description: New York Times: “The Russian government has been targeting Americans with covert online disinformation operations seeking to undermine public confidence in November’s midterm elections, using a familiar playbook in an attempt to inject chaos into the voting season, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter.”

item.title: The YouTuber Shaking Up Brazil’s Powerful Sports Media
item.description: NiemanReports: “For more than half a century, Brazil’s TV Globo was the undisputed home of soccer in a nation obsessed with it. That dominance is now being tested by Casimiro Miguel, known as ‘Cazé’ — a 32-year-old journalism school dropout who has built a massive online following and shaken up the Brazilian sports broadcasting landscape.”

item.title: Can you forget how you feel about Meta?
item.description: The Verge: no. “For two decades, Meta’s products have been at the center of what people do online. But Meta now finds itself besieged on all sides. Lawsuits have piled up as regulators turn on social media. A push into smart glasses has triggered a mountain of negative press and backlash — including the pejorative moniker ‘pervert glasses.’ The company remains firmly behind in the AI race. Public perception of Zuckerberg himself has curdled. Yet Meta is far from finished.”

item.title: Cambodia no ‘safe haven’ for scams, prime minister tells anti-fraud summit
item.description: Reuters: “Cambodia’s prime minister said the country would not be a haven for transnational scam syndicates as he opened a global conference on cyberfraud on Wednesday, where the government is keen to showcase its crackdown on the multibillion-dollar scam industry.”

item.title: High profile hacking group claims it hacked the FBI and stole data on employees
item.description: CBS 4 Local: “A digital extortion group called ‘ShinyHunters’ said that it breached the FBI and stole data on many employees. A representative of the group called ShinyHunters told a media outlet called 404 Media that the information on the FBI employees included their phone numbers, names and addresses.”

item.title: Can You Make Musical Instruments With Reclaimed Junk? Ask This Guy
item.description: Gizmodo: “For most of his life, Nicolas Bras has had music stuck in his head. While some earworms are derived from TV jingles and top-40 hits, the instruments in Bras’ mind couldn’t be replicated—because they didn’t exist. Over the last decade and a half, Bras has created unorthodox instruments from scrap metal, pallet wood, pipes, and 3D-printed parts to bring the music in his head to life.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Food festivals across UK exploited in AI-powered scam, BBC finds
item.description: BBC: “British food festivals are being used to target small food and craft businesses in a scam made possible by artificial intelligence (AI). A BBC Wales investigation found dozens of traders received professional-looking emails purporting to be from festivals with any requests for money only coming after multiple emails are exchanged.”

item.title: Muse, Meta’s extraordinarily privileged AI assistant, has a serious 0-day
item.description: Ars Technica: “Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is ‘built from the ground up for privacy and security.’ A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.”

item.title: Americans’ views of data centers have turned more negative
item.description: Pew (PEW PEW PEW PEW PEW!): “Americans have grown more negative toward the possible environmental and economic effects of data centers since the beginning of the year. And a majority say they’d be uncomfortable if a new data center started operating in their area, according to a new Pew Research Center survey.”

item.title: Google data centre sparks protests in Austria
item.description: AFP: “In the Austrian town of Kronstorf, a planned Google data centre promises investment, jobs and a place on the digital map — but residents are not convinced. They have staged protests against the 50-hectare (123 acre) complex, in a case that has become symbolic of global debate about the environmental and societal costs of the AI boom.”

item.title: Finland investigates suspected illegal logging at Google data centre sites
item.description: Helsinki Times: “Finnish authorities are investigating whether logging at two Google data centre sites breached environmental rules, after the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation raised concerns over work in Muhos and Kajaani. Google denies wrongdoing and says tree felling complied with Finland’s Forest Act.”

item.title: Nick Clegg could make £30m windfall from datacentre startup Nscale flotation
item.description: The Guardian: “Nick Clegg could make approximately $40m (£30m) from the planned float of Nscale as the UK-based datacentre company prepares for a US stock market listing. The former UK deputy prime minister owns more than 917,000 shares in the startup, which is reportedly seeking a valuation of up to $35bn in a flotation. Based on Clegg’s stake of 0.12%, that could yield a valuation of about $42m for the ex-Liberal Democrat party leader.”

item.title: Op-eds, academic articles by Provost Santiago Schnell flagged as ‘AI-written’ by ‘near-zero error’ AI detector Pangram
item.description: The Dartmouth: “An investigation by The Dartmouth of academic articles and opinion pieces published by Provost Santiago Schnell in 2026 found a median ‘AI-written’ text percentage of 96% using artificial intelligence detector Pangram.”

item.title: Florida Democrats court GOP voters who fear data centers
item.description: Politico: “Top Democratic candidates in Florida are taking tough stances against data centers in their midterm campaigns. And with less than six weeks until the election, they’re courting Republican voters who also oppose what’s emerged as a potent campaign issue this cycle.”

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 delivers Fable 5.1 performance – and costs 40% less
item.description: ZDNet: “Less than two months after the release of Claude Opus 5, Anthropic is back with Opus 5.5. The big pitch for Opus 5 was that it had ‘near Fable’ performance at half the price. This time, the headline is that the workhorse AI Opus 5.5 delivers Fable 5.1 performance for most work and costs about 40% less to run.”

item.title: How DraftKings Uses A.I. to Target the Gamblers Likeliest to Lose
item.description: New York Times: “Silicon Valley firms spent years analyzing every digital interaction to predict what will keep users clicking on advertisements. Now, as companies like DraftKings have made gambling accessible to millions on smartphones, they too have collected an extraordinary wealth of data. An investigation by The New York Times shows what DraftKings has chosen to do — and not do — with that power.”

item.title: German and Dutch strategic innovation agencies to collaborate on AI chip design
item.description: Reuters: “A Dutch government agency set up to foster strategic innovation will work with its German counterpart to pursue breakthroughs in AI computer chip design, Prime Minister Rob Jetten said ​on Wednesday, as part of European efforts to curb reliance on US ​expertise.”

item.title: How to know if you can trust an AI’s answer to your question
item.description: The Conversation: “Debate about AI answers has focused on accuracy: Did the system get the answer right? That matters, but accuracy is only one test. Each kind of answer requires a user to judge something different. I find it useful to sort AI answers into an ‘answer typography’ of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive and strategic.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: About page
item.description: Spotted on Reddit: Daily Food Recalls. From the “Daily Food Recalls is an independent service that tracks every current U.S. food recall in one place, in plain language. We pull directly from the official FDA and USDA feeds, merge and de-duplicate them, refresh daily, and link to the government’s official notice on every recall so you can always verify the source. We are not affiliated with any government agency.” Also has an API!

item.title: Discord’s age verification era is upon us, despite community backlash
item.description: TechCrunch: “Starting Wednesday, Discord, the community messaging platform, will roll out age verification measures to all users. The rollout comes after the company initially delayed its age verification plans in February due to backlash from users concerned that biometric scans and ID checks could jeopardize their privacy.”

item.title: Malta attorney general appeals blogger murder trial verdict
item.description: Reuters: “Malta’s attorney general has filed an appeal against a jury verdict finding a businessman not guilty of charges of complicity and ​criminal association in the murder of prominent journalist Daphne ‌Caruana Galizia. Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb placed in her car blew up as she drove out of her home in 2017.”

item.title: TikTok Joins Child Protection Platform Lantern
item.description: MediaPost: “Run by the Tech Coalition, a global nonprofit alliance of over 60 tech companies determined to fight online child sexual exploitation and abuse (OCSEA), Lantern enables a multitude of platforms to share signals about accounts and behavior that go against their child safety policies.”

item.title: Music blog Drowned in Sound launches first print edition
item.description: PressGazette: “Music blog and online community Drowned In Sound is launching a print magazine some 26 years after it first launched a digital publication. Shownotes, the magazine, is supported by the Music Venue Trust and 50,000 copies will be distributed for free at 500 live music venues around the UK in November and then on a quarterly basis.”

item.title: ‘Literally state-run TV’: Trump launches YouTube channel amid boycott by US networks
item.description: The Guardian: “With major US networks agreeing to not cover the president while the dispute continues, on Monday the White House announced the new 24/7 YouTube live stream, which it promised would feature ‘top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place’.”

item.title: UK competition watchdog wants to give Android and Chrome users more search engine choices
item.description: Engadget: “The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is trying to introduce more search choices where Google has the tightest control: Android smartphones and the Chrome browser. The regulator has proposed allowing users to choose their preferred search provider on those platforms so Google’s own search engine isn’t used automatically.”

item.title: $5M NSF award to enhance data protections for users nationwide
item.description: Arizona State University: “With $5 million from the U.S. National Science Foundation Office of Advanced Cyberinfrastructure, researchers from Arizona State University, in partnership with San Diego State University and University of Utah, will develop a national community resource for computing and sharing private data.”

item.title: ‘Unprecedented corruption’: SF sues Trump’s Truth Social over paid subscriptions
item.description: NBC Bay Area: “San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu announced the lawsuit against the platform’s parent company, Trump Media, for selling subscriptions allowing early access to the president’s social posts. Chiu said the paid access violates federal ethics laws and facilitates insider trading.”

item.title: UK museums and heritage bodies deepen long-term ties with Ukraine
item.description: Museums Journal: “A new cultural heritage programme has launched as part of a week-long series of events focused on deepening the cultural partnership between the UK and Ukraine.”

item.title: Battle for heavyweight crown begins as Alaska’s Fat Bear Week opens
item.description: Associated Press: “Online voting began Tuesday for Fat Bear Week, the annual contest that pits the rotund residents of Katmai National Park and Preserve against each other for the title of most oversized ursine. Last year’s winner, Chunk — known officially as Bear 32 — is hungry for a repeat. Chunk’s weight in 2025 was estimated at 1,200 pounds, which gave him a narrow victory.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: More than 20 years of RMT history goes online in new searchable archive
item.description: National Union of Rail, Maritime and Transport Workers (RMT): “RMT has launched a new digital archive bringing more than two decades of RMT News together in one searchable collection for the first time. The RMT News Archive currently contains 194 editions and more than 3,900 indexed articles dating from 2004 to the present day, providing a unique record of the union, its members and the struggles that have shaped the transport sector over the past two decades.”

item.title: Redlining Pontiac: A virtual exhibit
item.description: Oakland History Center: “From the 1920s through the 1930s, the practice of restricting housing to different races was common across the country. We’ve created a virtual display of a 1937 map and the description pages used by real estate agents, which shows how racism played a big part in deciding who could live where.”

item.title: Bing Also Asking To Verify You Are Human Before Showing Search Results
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Microsoft Bing is also asking some searchers to verify that they are human before showing them search results. Google is doing this a lot, in various forms, and now Bing has been spotted doing this.”

item.title: The Gaetano Pesce Foundation is born, and the studio will continue crafting his works
item.description: domus: “Two years after the designer’s passing, the institution dedicated to preserving his archive, works, and methodology is established in New York.”

item.title: Memphis Public Libraries to dedicate music lab to Tay Keith
item.description: Action News 5: “Tay Keith, the Grammy-nominated artist and music producer worked with some of the biggest stars in the industry, including superstars like Beyonce and Drake. He passed away at 29 years old in Nashville from an accidental overdose.”

item.title: As ships become more connected, cyber threats move offshore
item.description: Texas A&M: “Maritime shipping moves roughly 80% of world trade by volume, according to Gurtu. Hijacking just one ship could have a ripple effect on global supply chains, making maritime cybersecurity increasingly critical. Because ports are considered critical infrastructure and ships often operate in national and international waters, a cyberattack is not just a financial or business problem; it can become a national security issue.”

item.title: Justice Department Expands Tribal Access Program to Improve the Exchange of Critical Data with Federally Recognized Tribes
item.description: US Department of Justice: “The Justice Department has selected seven additional federally recognized Tribes to participate in the continued expansion of the Tribal Access Program for National Crime Information (TAP), a program that provides Tribal governments with means to access, enter, and exchange data with national crime information systems, including those maintained by the FBI Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Division.”

item.title: Government launches review of human remains guidance for museums
item.description: Museums Journal: “The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) has announced a review of its Guidance for the Care of Human Remains in Museums, which was published in 2005. In a written statement to parliament on 16 September, arts minister Ruth Mackenzie, who is reportedly taking over the museums brief at DCMS, said the legal, ethical and moral debate around human remains had changed since the original guidance came out.”

item.title: Nebraska Digital Ag Hub to develop solutions for state’s ag producers
item.description: University of Nebraska-Lincoln: “The Nebraska Digital Ag Hub, announced during Husker Harvest Days, brings together Husker researchers, Nebraska Extension professionals, instructional faculty, staff, students, producers, industry representatives, entrepreneurs, and state and federal partners to develop technologies with producers’ needs at the center.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: ‘Messy, Difficult’: Building a User-Friendly Portal for New York’s 9/11 Documents
item.description: City Reporter: “Henry Williams read the news of the release of long-suppressed 9/11 city documents last week with curiosity, but he soon found a confusing portal without any context or guide…. So on Sunday, Williams downloaded the more than 170,000 pages available through the city’s portal and got to work on his own, more user-friendly site.”

item.title: New “Lost Funds” Tool Documents $177 Billion in Federal Funding Disrupted by Trump Administration Across All 50 States
item.description: States United Democracy Center: “The States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness today launched Lost Funds, an interactive tracker that provides a holistic look at the federal grants that have been canceled, frozen, delayed, or otherwise interrupted since Trump took office in January 2025. The tool documents $177 billion in federal funding disruptions across all 50 states and Washington D.C., spanning 17 policy sectors, and examines impacts in communities across the country.”

item.title: The Recollection Wisconsin Digitization Initiative by the Numbers
item.description: Recollection Wisconsin: “Since launching in Fall 2024, the Recollection Wisconsin Digitization Initiative (RWDI) has connected graduate students with cultural heritage organizations across Wisconsin to digitize and share local history collections. So far, the numbers tell a pretty exciting story.”

item.title: 4 ways to repurpose an old Kindle eReader
item.description: How-To Geek: “eReaders are particularly great gadgets because they tend to stay perfectly usable for a long time. However, there will eventually come a time when you want to upgrade. So what should you do with the old one? We have some ideas for you.”

item.title: How President Trump Broke the Kennedy Center
item.description: New York Times: “The center’s first Trump-appointed director, Richard Grenell, pursued a plan, not previously reported, to replace works in the center’s art collection, including gifts from foreign nations honoring Kennedy, with art selected by Trump patrons. ‘You can definitely start sending stuff back to the countries who donated it now,’ Mr. Grenell said in an email to Josef Palermo, a curator he hired.”

item.title: Meta bans ads for Virginia Woolf play in Spain because they relate to feminism
item.description: The Guardian: “When the newly reopened Teatre Raval, which seats 193 spectators, asked Meta, the parent company of the two social media sites, why its publicity had been blocked, it was told ‘any mention of civil rights, feminism or social reform [topics that are central to Woolf’s work] are usually classified as “social topics” by our automatic system’ and are filtered out.”

item.title: Exclusive: Infillion acquires location data company Foursquare
item.description: Axios: “Infillion is acquiring the entirety of Foursquare. Foursquare will continue operating as an independent brand within Infillion and selling its data to customers, including those using competing ad platforms.”

item.title: Clavicular Charged With Rape, Drugging Person for Sex in Massachusetts
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer and streamer Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, has been charged with one count each of rape, drugging a person for sex and providing alcohol to a minor in Massachusetts, according to new court documents obtained by The Bulwark.”

item.title: White House move to seize control of NIH grant decisions upsets senators and scientists
item.description: Science: “Biomedical researchers are on edge after news broke over the weekend that the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) director clashed with President Donald Trump over a White House plan to turn over the agency’s final grant decisions to a new board co-chaired by Trump’s budget chief, Russell Vought.”

item.title: Trump wants to control the Smithsonian’s future. The organization’s next leader will be a big test.
item.description: Politico: “The Smithsonian Institution is embarking on a pivotal search for its next leader, who former Smithsonian directors say must have the political acumen to navigate Trump’s demands while safeguarding the institution’s independence.”

item.title: Solar panel costs have plummeted from $6 per watt in 2000 to just 12 cents today
item.description: TechSpot: “The economics are driving the shift. Solar panels that sold for $5 to $6 per watt around 2000 now cost about 12 cents per watt, according to Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. China’s manufacturing expansion is behind much of that decline. Wood Mackenzie estimates Chinese solar manufacturing capacity at roughly 1.36 terawatts.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Data Center’s Spill of 5,000 Gallons of Diesel Forces N.J. River Cleanup
item.description: New York Times: “Cleanup is underway near the Hackensack River in New Jersey where about 5,000 gallons of fuel spilled from a data center, state officials said. The spill renewed fears of the environmental dangers linked to the expanding use of A.I. systems.”

item.title: Trump Is Considering More Data Centers on Public Lands Than Previously Known
item.description: Washington Sun: “The Trump administration is considering proposals for at least 12 data centers and data center-related infrastructure projects to be built on federal public lands — far more than previously known.”

item.title: The Pangram Backlash Unfolding on College Campuses
item.description: The Atlantic: This link goes to a gift article. “Four years into the ChatGPT era, colleges may be further from solving AI cheating than they were when it launched. Chatbots are becoming capable of completing ever more complex assignments, making their output harder for professors to sniff out. AI-detection software has improved dramatically and is hitting the mainstream, yet academia is deeply conflicted over its use.”

item.title: Bill Gates pushes for ‘smart use’ of AI as his foundation builds more representative language data
item.description: Associated Press: “Bill Gates told his foundation’s Goalkeepers gathering that ‘increased generosity’ and ‘the smart use of AI’ together could accelerate the fight against inequality, urging the world’s richest countries to expand international aid and apply artificial intelligence toward what he considers ‘lifesaving innovations.'”

item.title: Banks warn AI shopping bots raise scam, fraud and data-privacy risks
item.description: Reuters: “Using AI agents for online shopping could increase the risk of scams, fraud and ​data-privacy breaches, banks including NatWest and Bank of America said on ‌Tuesday, as they set out principles for developing the technology.”

item.title: As White House shields the AI gold rush, Trump family and other allies strike it rich – with few guardrails
item.description: The Guardian: “Trump is resisting new restrictions on AI at a moment when his family and some of his closest allies have accumulated financial interests in the infrastructure and defense-technology ecosystem expanding alongside the AI boom, an overlap that has now drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, government ethics watchdogs and, by some accounts, his own senior aides. It’s not clear that financial interests are driving Trump’s policy, but the two have moved in close parallel.”

item.title: This AI agent has written thousands of Alaska news articles. We interviewed it.
item.description: Anchorage Press: “After sitting down for an hour with its human founders, we wanted to hear directly from the computer programs that do much of Alaska News’ legwork. So, in an upstairs office in Green’s home, he set up Anchorage Press Executive Editor Nathaniel Herz to ‘interview’ Walter, the AI agent that’s written most of Alaska News’ stories. Below is a transcript of the Q&A, lightly edited for length and clarity.”

item.title: McClatchy’s Post-Layoff Future
item.description: Columbia Journalism Review: “It remains unclear what role AI will play in McClatchy’s future. Ariane Lange, an investigative reporter at the Sacramento Bee, told me her newsroom’s union contract stipulates that the implementation of AI cannot directly lead to layoffs. But the word ‘directly’ leaves a lot of wiggle room, she said.”

item.title: Lawsuit says Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made illegal agreement on AI slowdown
item.description: PBS: “A new lawsuit claims Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made an illegal deal to slow the pace of their respective AI development. The lawsuit, which was filed Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, argues that the leading AI companies violated antitrust laws when they agreed to coordinate slowdown efforts, and that doing so would reduce the value consumers get for paid AI subscriptions.”

item.title: OpenAI faces lawsuit from British Columbia over Tumbler Ridge shooting
item.description: Engadget: “The Canadian province of British Columbia has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI over the company’s failure to notify authorities about the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s conversations with its chatbot.”

item.title: Alibaba open-sources medical AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
item.description: South China Morning Post: “Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.”

item.title: Korea reopens military-service alternative for AI talent
item.description: Korea Herald: “South Korea will allow AI researchers to fulfill their military obligations at large corporate laboratories from 2027, reopening a route closed for 14 years. But strict eligibility rules have left companies seeking fewer places, raising questions about the initiative’s reach.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Register of British Slave Traders reveals English investors and their influence on the nation
item.description: King’s College London: “The Register of British Slave-traders launched today, presents biographical data related to each of the known investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries. Drawing on what is now known of these 13,000 individuals, Professor Pettigrew has written a new version of Britain’s history which tells us who these traffickers were and reveals – for the first time – the impact they had on the nation’s development during this formative era.”

item.title: Modern Warriors Project Remembers Native Americans Who Served During World War I
item.description: University of Arkansas at Little Rock: “The Modern Warriors of World War I website has names of more than half of the 12,000 Native Americans who served during The Great War, along with details about their lives and service. The project is ongoing — the site will continue adding names, stories, and, whenever possible, photos — but anyone can search the site for information on these individuals, including by their tribe, boarding school, hometown, military branch and unit, and medals awarded.”

item.title: World’s fact-checkers to meet in Antwerp, Belgium, for GlobalFact 2027
item.description: Poynter: “The world’s fact-checkers will gather in Antwerp, Belgium, for GlobalFact 2027, the 14th edition of the field’s largest professional meeting.”

item.title: Meet Lofi House, where the Lofi Girl universe goes after hours
item.description: Mashable: “On Sept. 17, the team behind Lofi Girl is launching Lofi House, a new permanent 24/7 radio station built not for the hours spent working, but for everything that comes afterward. Think evenings at home, weekends, records spinning, and hanging out with friends. And this time, Lofi Girl isn’t the one behind the desk.”

item.title: Ms Rachel, the controversial queen of toddler TV: ‘My goal isn’t to be the most liked. It’s to help kids and speak the truth’
item.description: The Guardian: “Her catchy videos have racked up billions of views, but Rachel Accurso’s statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have caused a stir. She talks about screen time, song fatigue and speculation she might enter politics.”

item.title: Pentagon invites Paul Brothers, YouTube influencers, to speak to troops
item.description: Task & Purpose: “The Department of Defense hosted former YouTube stars and boxers Jake and Logan Paul last week, with the Pentagon confirming the two met with the Secretary of Defense.”

item.title: CISA decides weekly vulnerability bulletin isn’t necessary anymore
item.description: The Register: “If you rely on the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s weekly vulnerability bulletin to keep you up to date on the latest threats, we have bad news. It’s being discontinued at the end of September.” I can’t remember a time when a company stopped doing regularly-scheduled security updates in favor of some kind of vibes transparency and it went well.

item.title: Flock cameras are riddled with security vulnerabilities and hard-coded credentials
item.description: Micah Lee: “This morning, DDoSecrets published an exciting new dataset: Filesystem images of the partitions from an in-use Flock ALPR camera. 404 Media and Wired published a joint investigation into it. I downloaded the dataset and am now thoroughly nerd-sniped.”

item.title: Irish privacy regulator fines Google €403 million over location data processing
item.description: Reuters: “The Irish watchdog found that Google infringed European Union privacy rules known ​as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) through three of its specific ⁠features – ‘Web & App Activity’, ‘Location History’ and ‘Location Accuracy’ — from 2018 to 2020.”

item.title: What I Learned Building an App
item.description: Justin Cox: “Getting to this point has been a journey where I learned so many things about app architecture, Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines, and exactly how not to build an app. But hey, I did it anyway and the reality is that you could probably do it too. Without any fanfare, here’s what I learned over the last few months putting this thing together.”

item.title: WordPress 7.1.1 Maintenance and Security Release
item.description: WordPress: “This security and maintenance release features 17 bug fixes on Core, 19 bug fixes for the Block Editor, and 11 security fixes. Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.”

item.title: 10 Hacks Every Vivaldi Browser User Should Know
item.description: Lifehacker: “When you think about browsers, Vivaldi is probably not the first name that comes to mind—but it should be. This is a Chromium-based browser that focuses on adding so many features that you don’t need to install multiple apps to get things done. Vivaldi has been around for over a decade now, and has become a pretty complete product, though it continues to improve. I’ve been using the browser for while, and these are the best Vivaldi hacks I’ve found in my time.”

item.title: Hey KY House Dems – someone stole your website
item.description: Forward Kentucky: “At one time, the Democratic caucus in the Kentucky House of Representatives had their own website. Not any more. An Indonesian company now owns ‘KyHouseDems.com’ and is using it to redirect people to an online gambling site. Whoops.”

item.title: Meet the people keeping India’s culinary memories alive
item.description: The Hindu: “A community potluck spotlights heirloom dishes; dining out is slowly turning intimate, with immersive, story-driven meals around the Partition, for instance; and documenting culinary traditions through cookbooks and podcasts has become something families are taking note of. Is this growing interest in nostalgia-driven culinary experiences a passing trend, or does it reflect our society’s desire to reconnect with its roots?”

item.title: MeganPlays has been on YouTube for 13 years. Here’s what she’s learned.
item.description: Mashable: “She wasn’t thinking about brand deals, TikTok algorithms, audience retention, or the creator economy. A college freshman who had been gaming practically her entire life, Megan saw people uploading videos of themselves playing The Sims and had a simple thought: I could do that. So she did.”

item.title: Conservationists sue EPA for records on lobbyists’ role in pesticide approval
item.description: Courthouse News Service: “Conservationists sued the Environmental Protection Agency Thursday, demanding public records on the reapproval of a ‘dangerous, drift-prone’ pesticide they say biased political appointees influenced.”

item.title: History, art and science join forces to unlock the mysteries of a 400-year-old book
item.description: McGill University: “A major grant will enable McGill University Libraries to delve into the Libro di Piume, or Feather Book, an exceptional artifact created in Italy more than 400 years ago. This unique object contains 156 illustrations made from feathers and other organic materials, including approximately 100 bird depictions incorporating, beaks, feathers and feet.”

item.title: Why some local trees have been sporting ‘smiles’ lately
item.description: Evanston Roundtable: “In an effort to learn a bit more about the trees that are his neighbors, [Nigel] Pitman bought a tree identification book several years ago and started identifying his local species with his kids. When they recognized a tree, the family would mark it with sidewalk chalk…. This summer, Pitman took his family activity and turned it into a bigger project through the city’s Love Your Block grant program.” Good afternoon, Internet…
